newsitem.title: USA: Swiss made restitution offer -- Jewish group.
newsitem.headline: Swiss made restitution offer -- Jewish group.

text.p: The Swiss government was receptive to a Jewish proposal that it make a good faith financial gesture to Holocaust victims and even proposed a payment of $250 million, a Jewish source close to the negotiations said.
The source spoke on Tuesday to rebut a charge by a former Swiss president that the request for a good faith gesture amounted to blackmail and extortion.
The Swiss government, refusing to rebuke its ex-president, said it wanted to use $30 million in dormant Jewish accounts in Swiss banks to start a Holocaust memorial fund.

The proposal led to an outcry from some Jewish groups that the Swiss government wanted to set up a fund with money that was not theirs. But the Jewish group charged with negotiating with the Swiss had no immediate comment.

The World Jewish Restitution Organization, headed by World Jewish Congress President Edgar Bronfman, declined comment and instead set early February as the time in which it will hold a special session to decide what action to take. The group has several options under consideration -- including calling for a boycott of Swiss banks.

In making the fund proposal, the Swiss Federal Council ignored Jewish demands that it rebuke Economics Minister Jean-Pascal Delamuraz, for labelling their calls for compensation "extortion and blackmail." Delamuraz made his comment while he was still Switzerland's president.
"There was no apology by the Federal Council because the remarks (by Delamuraz) were misunderstood and led to excessive reactions," government spokesman Achille Casanova said.

The source close to the negotiations said Jewish groups proposed last year that Switzerland make a good faith financial gesture for alleged profiteering during the Holocaust, but never attached a figure to that gesture. Many Jews had secret Swiss accounts during the Nazi era which they or their survivors were unable to retrieve after the war.

The source said the Swiss responded favorably to the fund idea and in a meeting in Switzerland with WJC representatives and later in New York with Bronfman, a Swiss government representative made the suggestion of a $250 million payment to start the fund. The New York meeting with Bronfman came just two weeks before Delamuraz's statement, the source said.
New York Republican Senator Alfonse D'Amato, the head of the Senate Banking Committee, sent a letter on Tuesday to new Swiss President Arnold Koller demanding he repudiate his predecessor's remarks.

"These remarks clearly do not serve the effort to rectify the injustices of the past. Most importantly, the silence of the Federal Council on the seriousness of the remarks is a telling feature of the country's policy in this regard," D'Amato said.
